turns.doctor_question: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, they sent me here from the station. I was just... I was moving the airway bags into a pattern. I knew it was the right pattern. Airway bags are heavy if you pack them wrong, you know? We had this one rookie who used to stuff the oxygen tubing in the wrong pocket and it would always get tangled. I hate tangled tubing. It reminds me of Christmas lights. My dad used to make me untangle the Christmas lights every single year in the freezing cold out in our garage... 

But anyway, I was putting the bags in the sequence and repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. Just saying them. You have to say them or they get lost in the air. Kind of like radio static. Do you ever just listen to the static on the radio? Sometimes it sounds exactly like ocean waves. I went to the ocean once in Florida when I was ten, got a terrible sunburn on my shoulders... 

But yeah, my lieutenant, he came over and told me to stop. He told me to step away from the bags. But I couldn't. I wouldn't step away because if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad. The whole ambulance bay would just go completely bad. So... he made me come here.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech and loose associations, jumping from the topic of airway bags to Christmas lights, and from radio static to a childhood sunburn.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes engaging in inappropriate, bizarre behavior at work (arranging bags into a pattern, repeating numbers) and refusing to stop when ordered by a superior.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes performing repetitive behaviors (arranging bags in a sequence, repeating dispatch numbers) to prevent a dreaded, unrealistic outcome (the ambulance bay 'going bad').

turns.doctor_question: Did you truly believe that if you stopped the sequence, the ambulance bay would go bad?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yeah, of course. It's not just a belief, it's a fact. If the sequence breaks, it all falls apart. You have to keep things exact, especially at the station. Like with the paperwork... I know the injury review people and some of the supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras. They watch me, and then they go in and change my triage notes. They do it on purpose to make me look unsafe on the job. They tell me, "Oh, it's just routine paperwork, don't worry about it," but I know they're altering my notes. 

Paperwork used to be so much simpler before they switched to those new tablets, anyway. The screens are always way too bright. It hurts your eyes if you stare at it too long, kind of like staring at the snow when the sun is out. We had this massive blizzard back in '09, and the snow was piled up completely past the headlights on the rig. We were slipping all over the roads. I had to shovel my entire driveway that week with this flimsy plastic shovel because my neighbor borrowed my good metal one and never gave it back. He said he lost it in his garage, but how do you lose a bright red snow shovel? You really can't trust people when you lend them tools.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that supervisors are watching them through cameras and maliciously altering their triage notes to make them look unsafe.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from discussing paperwork and tablets to a past blizzard and a neighbor borrowing a snow shovel.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Have you been hearing voices when no one is actually there?
turns.patient_response: Voices? No, I don't hear anybody talking when it's empty. Just the regular sounds, you know? Unless you count the dispatch radio, but that's a real voice. Although sometimes the static on the radio sounds a little bit like whispering if the volume is turned down too low. Whispering always reminds me of the library. I practically lived in the library when I was getting my associate's degree. They had these big, heavy wooden tables that always smelled like lemon polish. I really hate the smell of lemon polish. It smells exactly like those cheap air fresheners they hang in the station bathrooms. We ran out of paper towels in the bathroom last Tuesday and nobody even bothered to restock them. I had to dry my hands on my uniform pants, which is a terrible idea because then the fabric gets all stiff and uncomfortable. Kind of like when you wash your uniform and forget to use fabric softener. Do you use fabric softener? My mom always swore by the lavender kind, but I think it just makes the inside of the washing machine completely gummy.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, wandering from radio static to libraries, lemon polish, bathrooms, and fabric softener.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices when no one is there, stating they only hear regular sounds or real voices on the radio.

turns.doctor_question: Have there been times when you felt unusually high, euphoric, or intensely energetic?
turns.patient_response: Energetic? No, I don't... I don't really get like that. I'm mostly just tired from the shifts. A lot of the guys at the station drink those huge energy drinks to stay awake, the ones in the tall cans? I tried the green one once, but it made my teeth feel completely fuzzy. I really hate when my teeth feel fuzzy. It's exactly like when you eat too much spinach. My mom used to make this baked spinach casserole every single Thanksgiving and it was always so watery. I don't understand why people put vegetables in casseroles anyway, it just ruins the texture. Texture is really important with food. Like pudding, you know? I can't eat pudding unless it's completely smooth. They used to give us pudding cups in middle school, but the plastic spoons they had in the cafeteria were always so flimsy they'd just snap right in half if you pressed too hard. Have you ever tried to eat with a broken plastic spoon? It's basically impossible. You just end up getting it all over your fingers, and then your hands are sticky all afternoon. I hate having sticky hands, it makes it impossible to grip the steering wheel properly.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, wandering off-topic from energy drinks to spinach casseroles, pudding, and plastic spoons.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient explicitly denies feeling unusually high or euphoric.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly denies feeling intensely energetic, stating they do not get like that.

turns.doctor_question: When you were a child, did you have a hard time making friends?
turns.patient_response: Friends? Um, I don't really know. I guess I didn't think about it much back then. I was mostly just doing my own thing, you know? Playing in the dirt, building forts... I built this really amazing fort once out of these old wooden pallets I found behind the grocery store. The grocery store near my house always threw out the best boxes, too. The thick cardboard ones they use for the bananas. Bananas are such a weird fruit if you think about it. They come in their own wrapper, but if you leave them on the counter for even one extra day, they get all brown and mushy. My partner at the station always eats brown bananas. He says they're sweeter, but I just can't get past the smell. It smells exactly like the inside of a dumpster in July. We had to park the rig next to a dumpster last week during a call, and the smell completely seeped into the cab. We had to drive with the windows down the whole way back, which was freezing because the heater on our side is completely busted. I told the mechanic about it three times, but he never listens to me. He just writes it down on his little clipboard and walks away. I hate clipboards. They always pinch your fingers if you aren't careful.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response exhibits severe tangentiality and derailment, shifting rapidly from childhood friends to forts, grocery stores, bananas, a coworker, a dumpster, a broken heater, and finally clipboards, demonstrating disorganized thinking and speech.

turns.doctor_question: When you were a child, did you often need things to be done in a very exact way?
turns.patient_response: Exact way? Um, I don't... I don't really remember needing things to be exact when I was little. I was just a kid, you know? But my partner at the station, he's obsessed with exactness. He organizes the jump bag the exact same way every single shift. If I put the trauma shears in the wrong pocket, he loses his mind. Trauma shears are actually pretty incredible tools if you think about it. They can cut right through a leather boot or even a penny. I tried cutting a penny once just to see if it worked, but it just bent it in half and then the penny got stuck in the blades. Have you ever gotten a coin stuck in a machine? There's this vending machine in the breakroom that always eats my quarters. I lost three dollars trying to get a bag of pretzels last month. Pretzels are the worst snack anyway, they just make you incredibly thirsty. And the water fountain by the breakroom has been broken since October. It just drips this tiny, lukewarm stream that tastes completely like rust. I can't stand the taste of rust. It reminds me of when you accidentally bite your lip too hard and you get that metallic taste in your mouth. I bit my lip last night while I was trying to eat a sandwich and it swelled up so much I could barely talk on the radio. The dispatcher kept asking me to repeat myself, which is incredibly annoying because the radio static is already so loud.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits marked tangentiality and loose associations, drifting continuously from the topic of exactness to trauma shears, pennies, vending machines, rust, and radio static.

turns.doctor_question: Do people often tell you that your speech is hard to follow or that you go off on tangents?
turns.patient_response: Hard to follow? No, I... I don't think so. People usually know what I'm talking about. The only time people can't follow me is over the radio, but like I said, the static is just terrible. The dispatchers have it easy because they get those really expensive headsets with the noise-canceling foam. I had to wear one of those foam headsets once for a training module, but the foam makes your ears sweat so much. It's exactly like wearing a wool sweater indoors. My grandmother knitted me a wool sweater when I was a teenager, but it was this awful scratchy yarn. It was supposed to be red, but it looked more like tomato soup. Tomato soup is really only good if you have a grilled cheese sandwich to dip in it, but you have to use the right kind of cheese. If you use that cheap plastic-wrapped cheese, it doesn't melt right, it just turns into this weird oily plastic layer. I left a plastic spatula too close to the stove burner once and it melted into a puddle on the counter. The smell of melting plastic is impossible to get out of a kitchen. We had to keep the windows open for three days, and the screens on the windows were completely rusted out. Bugs kept flying in, especially those little fruit flies. Fruit flies are so pointless, they just hover around the sink drain no matter how much bleach you pour down there. Bleach gives me a terrible headache anyway. It smells exactly like the hospital corridors at county general. We do patient drop-offs there all the time, and the automatic doors at the ambulance bay are always getting stuck halfway open. It's a huge fire hazard if you ask me.

symptom_reasoning.S021: Although the patient initially denies that their speech is hard to follow, their entire response is a clear demonstration of tangentiality and loose associations, wandering continuously from radio static to headsets, wool sweaters, tomato soup, melted plastic, fruit flies, and hospital doors.

turns.doctor_question: When you think the ambulance bay will go bad if the sequence is broken, does any part of you feel that this might not actually be true?
turns.patient_response:
Not true? No, I... I know it is true. That's exactly why they sent me here in the first place. At the station, I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern that I knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. Dispatch numbers are so incredibly long now, you know? They used to just be a few digits, but now they add all these letters and zone codes. It's exactly like reading a serial number off the back of a refrigerator. We had to move this massive refrigerator for a patient once, and the compressor on the back was completely coated in this thick, greasy dust. Dust always makes my nose itch right at the bridge, where my sunglasses sit. I have these polarized sunglasses that are great for driving, but they make all the windows on the other cars look like they have rainbows on them. 

Anyway, my lieutenant came over and told me to stop and step away from the bags, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't step away. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. The bay is already in terrible shape as it is. There's this massive oil stain in bay three that nobody ever bothers to clean up. You're supposed to use cat litter to soak up motor oil, but the county only buys that cheap clay kind that doesn't even clump. It just turns into this awful gray paste if it gets wet. I stepped in some gray paste on a call last Tuesday and it completely ruined the treads on my boots. Good work boots are so expensive to replace on our salary, and the uniform allowance doesn't even cover half of it. They send the allowance as a separate paper check instead of direct deposit, which is so outdated. I always lose paper checks in the center console of my truck.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions that they always lose their paper checks in the center console of their truck.
symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient demonstrates a fixed belief, explicitly stating 'I know it is true' that the ambulance bay would go bad if the sequence was broken.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from dispatch numbers to refrigerators, dust, sunglasses, cat litter, and paper checks.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes their abnormal and inappropriate behavior at the station, including refusing to step away when ordered by their lieutenant.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes performing repetitive behaviors (arranging bags into a pattern, repeating numbers) to prevent a dreaded event (the bay going bad).

turns.doctor_question: When did you first start believing that arranging things in a certain pattern could keep bad things from happening?
turns.patient_response: When did it start? Um, well, the stuff at the station... the behavior that got everybody all alarmed, and all the camera and paperwork stuff, that's been going on for about the last two months. Paperwork is just endless now, honestly. You have to fill out a triplicate form just to restock the oxygen tanks. The carbon copies always leave that weird blue smudge on the side of your hand. It's impossible to wash off with regular soap. You have to use that gritty orange pumice soap that mechanics use. My dad was a mechanic, he always smelled exactly like that orange soap and motor oil. He had this old Ford truck that he was always fixing up, but the transmission kept slipping. Transmissions are incredibly complicated, all those tiny gears and fluid. Transmission fluid is this bright cherry red color, it looks almost exactly like cough syrup. I took some cherry cough syrup last winter when I had a chest cold, but it just made me feel incredibly dizzy and I ended up sleeping for fourteen hours straight. Sleeping on the station cots is terrible for your back anyway. The mattresses are so incredibly thin you can feel the metal springs poking right through the vinyl cover. Vinyl gets so hot in the summer, you wake up completely drenched in sweat.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient acknowledges the timeline of the delusional belief asked about by the doctor, referring to it as the behavior that alarmed everyone.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from the initial topic to paperwork, soap, mechanics, transmissions, cough syrup, and mattresses without returning to the point.

turns.doctor_question: Before these last two months, had you been having problems like these for six months or more?
turns.patient_response: Before two months ago? Well, the whole thing actually started after I hurt my shoulder and ribs during an ambulance transfer about eight months ago. We were moving this bariatric patient down a narrow flight of stairs, and the stair chair completely jammed on the landing. Those stair chairs are supposed to have a smooth glide track, but the tracks get filled with all this grit and dirt from people's shoes. People wear the dirtiest shoes into their houses, it makes no sense to me. My mom always made us take our shoes off at the front door and leave them on this little rubber mat. The rubber mat had these little bristles on it that were supposed to scrape the mud off, but they just ended up trapping all the pine needles from the yard. Pine needles are impossible to sweep up, they just slide right under the broom bristles. You really need a good shop vac to get them all. Shop vacs are incredibly loud, though, they sound exactly like a jet engine taking off. I live right under the flight path for the regional airport, so I hear jet engines all day long. They rattle the windows so hard I had to put weather stripping around all the frames just to stop the shaking. Weather stripping is basically just sticky foam, and the adhesive always dries out and peels off after a few months. It's exactly like that cheap medical tape we use on the rig, the kind that won't stick to anything if the patient is even a little bit sweaty. Sweating is just a nightmare when you're wearing those heavy uniform shirts. The polyester blend they make us wear doesn't breathe at all.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from their initial injury to stair chairs, shoes, rubber mats, pine needles, shop vacs, jet engines, weather stripping, medical tape, and finally polyester shirts.

turns.doctor_question: Since these problems began after your injury eight months ago, have they been going on continuously ever since?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, continuously. Ever since I messed up my shoulder and ribs on that transfer eight months ago, it's just been going on and on. My shoulder still clicks sometimes when I reach up, you know? Like when I have to grab the trauma shears off the top shelf in the rig. Those shears are supposed to be able to cut through a penny, but I've never actually tried it. Who has a penny just lying around anymore? Nobody uses cash. Everything is on those little plastic cards with the chips in them. The chips get scratched up so easily, though. I had to replace my debit card three times last year because the chip reader at the gas station kept rejecting it. Gas stations always smell so strongly of diesel and old hot dogs. Those hot dogs just roll on those metal heaters for hours, they must be completely dried out inside. I tried to eat one on a night shift once and it gave me the worst heartburn. Heartburn feels exactly like you swallowed a hot coal. We carry antacids on the truck, but they're the chalky mint kind. Mint flavor always reminds me of toothpaste, and eating toothpaste is just a terrible idea. My little brother ate a whole tube of sparkle toothpaste when we were kids and my mom had to call poison control. Poison control operators are so calm, I don't know how they do it. They just sit in a room with headsets all day. Headsets always give me a headache right behind my ears if I wear them too long.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting continuously from their shoulder injury to trauma shears, pennies, credit cards, gas stations, hot dogs, toothpaste, and headsets without returning to the original topic.

turns.doctor_question: Since this started, have you been having trouble doing your job or taking care of yourself?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, trouble working. I can't work the ambulance anymore. They tried putting me on desk duty, doing notes and equipment checks, but I guess I got so unreliable with it that they just took me off the schedule completely. Schedules are so rigid anyway, you know? Like, you have to clock in exactly at 0600 or the biometric scanner flags you. Those fingerprint scanners are terrible, half the time they don't even read your print if your hands are dry. My hands are always dry because of that awful hand sanitizer we use on the rig. It smells exactly like cheap tequila. I went to Mexico once, Cabo, and the tequila there was amazing, not like the stuff here. The beaches were beautiful, but the sand gets absolutely everywhere. You find sand in your shoes months later. Shoes with good arch support are so expensive now, easily over a hundred dollars. A hundred dollars doesn't buy anything at the grocery store anymore, either. I haven't even been going to the store much, honestly. I've mostly stopped seeing friends or keeping up with things at home the way I used to. My apartment is just... I don't know. The dust bunnies under the couch are getting huge. Dust is mostly dead skin cells, which is kind of gross when you think about it. Skin cells are constantly shedding, millions of them every day. It's like we're constantly falling apart, just leaving little pieces of ourselves everywhere we go.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting rapidly from work schedules to hand sanitizer, tequila, vacations, sand, shoes, and dust.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient reports having stopped seeing friends and no longer keeping up with things at home, indicating social withdrawal and a loss of motivation for daily activities.

turns.doctor_question: Have other people told you that your face seems blank or that you show less emotion than you used to?
turns.patient_response: I don't really know about my face, honestly, because I don't really see anyone for them to tell me. Most days I just sit in my apartment. There's trash just sitting in the corner, and all this food still in the fridge. I used to cook all the time, but I just can't get myself to care or start anything anymore. I don't even call the guys for basketball like I used to. We used to play at the community center, and the floors there are so polished. They squeak so loud when you run in rubber soles. Rubber comes from trees, originally, which is wild to think about. You just tap a tree and get tires. We blow out tires on the rig all the time because the city never fills the potholes on the east side. Potholes fill up with water when it rains, and then they freeze overnight and expand. Ice is one of the only substances that expands when it freezes. Most things shrink when they get cold. Like the thermal blankets we keep in the trauma bays, they always feel so thin and small when you pull them out of the warmer. Warmers are basically just giant incubators. Incubators always remind me of those little baby chicks they hatch in elementary school science class. We had a heat lamp for ours, and it gave off this intense red glow. Red is the longest wavelength of visible light, you know. That's why stoplights are red, so you can see them through the fog. Fog rolling in off the river is so thick here in November.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe derailment and loose associations, drifting continuously from basketball to rubber, tires, ice, incubators, and fog.
symptom_reasoning.S023: The patient describes avolition ('can't get myself to care or start anything') and asociality ('don't really see anyone').
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient reports a clear loss of interest and motivation in previously enjoyed activities, such as cooking and playing basketball.
symptom_reasoning.S075: The patient describes social isolation, noting they do not see anyone and have stopped reaching out to friends.

turns.doctor_question: Before your shoulder injury eight months ago, had you ever had a whole month when you were convinced people were watching you or when you knew certain patterns could prevent bad things from happening?
turns.patient_response: No, nothing like that before the injury. Everything was completely normal until I messed up my shoulder. Shoulders are such complicated joints, you know? It's a ball and socket, but the socket is really shallow, which is why they dislocate so easily. We had a call once for a guy who dislocated his shoulder playing rugby. Rugby seems so brutal, no pads or helmets or anything. Football players wear all that armor, but they still get concussions all the time. Concussions are weird because your brain basically bruises itself against the inside of your skull. The skull is supposed to protect you, but sometimes it's the thing that hurts you. Like when people don't wear helmets on motorcycles. Motorcycles are basically just engines with wheels. My uncle had a Harley, and it was so loud you could feel it vibrating in your chest from a block away. Vibrations can actually loosen screws over time, which is why you have to keep checking the mounting brackets on the stretcher in the ambulance. If the stretcher isn't secure, it's a huge liability. Liability insurance for EMS is insanely expensive. Everything is expensive now, though. Have you seen the price of eggs lately?

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting continuously from their shoulder injury to rugby, concussions, motorcycles, ambulances, and finally the price of eggs.
symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies having beliefs that people were watching them prior to their injury.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient explicitly denies having thoughts or behaviors where they believed certain patterns could prevent bad things from happening.

turns.doctor_question: Did the strange beliefs start right after your shoulder injury?
turns.patient_response: No, not right after. The injury was a while ago. The camera and paperwork stuff, and the station behavior that got everyone all alarmed, that's only been going on for about the last two months. Two months isn't that long, but they really do have cameras everywhere now. The lenses are getting so tiny, you can barely even see them. They hide them in smoke detectors and exit signs. Exit signs always have to be illuminated by law, you know. Fire codes are super strict about that. If a bulb burns out in an exit sign, the fire marshal will write you up instantly. We had a fire marshal inspect the station once who was absolutely obsessed with extension cords. You aren't allowed to daisy-chain extension cords because it creates a massive fire hazard. Fires burn so hot they can melt the structural steel right out of a building. Steel is an alloy, mostly iron and carbon. Carbon is what diamonds are made of, which is crazy. It takes millions of years of pressure in the earth's crust to make a diamond. And then people pay thousands of dollars for a shiny rock just to put it on a ring. Rings are actually really dangerous to wear on the job. In EMS, they tell you not to wear rings because you could get it caught on the stretcher mechanism and deglove your whole finger. Degloving is exactly what it sounds like, and it's horrible. Just... taking off a glove. The gloves they buy for us are always tearing anyway. The city switched to this cheap nitrile brand to save a few cents a box.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses fixed, paranoid beliefs about tiny cameras being hidden everywhere, including in smoke detectors and exit signs.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates clear tangentiality and loose associations, drifting continuously from exit signs to fire codes, steel, diamonds, rings, degloving injuries, and finally nitrile gloves.

turns.doctor_question: Did something very stressful happen in your life shortly before these beliefs started?
turns.patient_response: No, I don't think so. I mean, nothing stressful right before that. The shoulder thing was months before, like I said. Stress is such a weird concept anyway, right? Like, the body doesn't know the difference between good stress and bad stress. It's all just cortisol and adrenaline. Adrenaline is epinephrine, and we push that all the time during codes. It basically jumpstarts the heart. The heart is just a pump, really, just muscle and valves. Valves can get so calcified as people get older. Calcium is good for your bones, though. You're supposed to drink milk, but a lot of people are lactose intolerant. Lactose is a sugar, and the enzyme lactase breaks it down. If you don't have the enzyme, it just ferments in your gut and causes all this gas. Gas prices are ridiculous right now. I remember when it was under two bucks a gallon. Gallons are such a weird measurement, we really should just switch to the metric system like the rest of the world. The metric system makes so much more sense because everything is in base ten. Ten is a nice, round number.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates clear derailment and loose associations, shifting rapidly from stress to adrenaline, the heart, calcium, milk, lactose, intestinal gas, gas prices, and the metric system.
symptom_reasoning.S081: The patient explicitly denies experiencing any stressful event shortly before the onset of their symptoms.

turns.doctor_question: For at least a month, have you felt like you just couldn’t get yourself to start or do things, even basic daily tasks?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, it's been like that. Most days I just sit in my apartment. There's trash in the corner, food still in the fridge going bad, and I just... I can't get myself to care or start anything. I don't even call the guys for basketball anymore, or cook like I used to. Cooking takes so much prep work, you know? Chopping vegetables and measuring spices. Spices used to be worth more than gold back in the day. People literally sailed across the ocean just to find peppercorns and nutmeg. Nutmeg can actually be hallucinogenic if you eat enough of it, which is crazy to think about. It's just sitting right there in the baking aisle next to the cinnamon. Cinnamon comes from the bark of a tree. Trees are amazing, how they pull water all the way up from the roots to the leaves against gravity. Gravity is a constant, 9.8 meters per second squared. That's why falls from a height are so dangerous in trauma calls. We had this one call where a guy fell off a roof cleaning his gutters. Gutters get so clogged with leaves in the fall. Fall is my favorite season because the air gets so crisp. Crisp apples are the best, especially Honeycrisp. They engineered Honeycrisp apples at a university in Minnesota, I think. Minnesota has all those lakes. They say it's the land of ten thousand lakes, but it's actually more than that. Water is so heavy, though. A gallon of water weighs over eight pounds.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting rapidly from cooking to spices, gravity, trauma calls, apples, and lakes.
symptom_reasoning.S023: The patient confirms avolition, stating they sit in their apartment with trash and rotting food because they 'can't get myself to care or start anything.'
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient describes a clear loss of interest and social withdrawal, noting they no longer call friends for basketball or cook like they used to.

turns.doctor_question: Did these strange beliefs come on suddenly, over just a few days?
turns.patient_response: No, it wasn't sudden like that. It wasn't just a few days. It kind of just... grew, you know? Like it crept up over time, over weeks. Weeks feel so long when you're just sitting there, but then you look at a calendar and realize how fast the year is going. Calendars are weird because we use the Gregorian one, but there are so many other ways to track time. Like the lunar calendar. The moon controls the tides, which is wild when you think about it. Just this giant rock in space pulling all the oceans back and forth. Oceans cover most of the earth, and we've barely even explored the bottom of them. There are fish down there that make their own light because it's so dark. Bioluminescence, they call it. Fireflies do that too, in the summer. I used to catch them in jars when I was a kid. You have to poke holes in the lid so they can breathe, obviously. Breathing is automatic, controlled by the brainstem. The medulla oblongata. We had to memorize all the parts of the brain for EMT training. Training was intense, lots of flashcards. Flashcards are made of paper, and paper comes from paper mills, and those places smell terrible. There was a paper mill a few towns over from where I grew up, and on windy days, you could smell it everywhere. Wind power is getting huge now, though. Those giant turbines they put up in fields. They look like they're moving slow, but the tips of those blades are actually spinning incredibly fast.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, jumping rapidly from calendars to the moon, oceans, fireflies, brain anatomy, paper mills, and wind turbines.

turns.doctor_question: From when the suspicious thoughts and the belief about the pattern first began, has it been six months yet?
turns.patient_response: No, not six months. The camera stuff, the paperwork, and how everyone at the station started acting weird... that's been going on for about the last two months. Two months is a decent amount of time, I guess. Sixty days. It's crazy how we divide time into days based on the earth spinning. The earth spins at like a thousand miles an hour at the equator, but we don't feel it because everything is moving with us, including the atmosphere. The atmosphere is mostly nitrogen, not oxygen, which surprises a lot of people. We give 100% oxygen on the rig sometimes, like with a non-rebreather mask. Those masks have those little flaps on the side so the exhaled air can get out. Exhaling is just getting rid of carbon dioxide, which is a waste product of cellular respiration. Cells are basically tiny factories. Mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell, everybody remembers that from high school biology. High school feels like a lifetime ago. I played football back then, defensive tackle. Football is rough on the joints, though. So many guys end up with bad knees. Knees are hinge joints, but they have a lot of complex ligaments holding them together. The ACL is the one everyone tears. Tearing a ligament is worse than breaking a bone sometimes, because bones heal better. Bones are constantly remodeling themselves, breaking down and building back up. It's called Wolff's law, I think. Law is a whole other field. Lawyers have to read so much case law, just stacks and stacks of books. Books are getting replaced by tablets now, though. Everyone just reads on a screen.

turns.doctor_question: When this started, did people say you suddenly seemed confused or that your behavior changed a lot from your usual self?
turns.patient_response: No, nobody said I was confused. I knew exactly what was going on, it wasn't confusion. My behavior changed because I was figuring it all out, not because I was losing my mind. The mind is a crazy thing, though. The brain uses about twenty percent of the body's energy, even though it's only like two percent of the weight. It runs on glucose. Glucose is basically sugar. We push D50, which is fifty percent dextrose, for diabetic emergencies when they're crashing. Crashing an ambulance is my biggest fear. You're driving this massive box on wheels, lights and sirens going, and people still don't pull over. They just stare at you in their rearview mirrors. Mirrors are coated with silver or aluminum on the back so they reflect light. Light travels at 186,000 miles per second. If you could travel at the speed of light, time would actually slow down for you relative to people on earth. Einstein proved that with relativity. Relativity makes you think about how everything is connected in the universe. The universe is expanding, they say, getting bigger every second. I wonder what it's expanding into, though. Like, what's outside of it? Space is a vacuum, so there's no sound. Sound needs a medium to travel through, like air or water. Water is H2O. Two hydrogens, one oxygen. Oxygen is what we need, but too much of it can actually be toxic. Oxygen toxicity can cause seizures. Seizures are terrifying to watch if you don't know what's happening. People bite their tongues and everything. Tongues are the strongest muscle in the body, pound for pound.
